subject: The World Around Us
period_schedule_display:
Period schedule:
  Row 1: 40 minutes × 8 periods = 320 minutes
Total: 8 periods · 5h 20min

periods.textbook_anchor: Singing Together — Discuss who the members of Bela's family are (p. 6)

time_bands.activity: The teacher reads aloud the opening of the chapter, introducing Bela, Banku Bhaiya, and little Bishu playing chhupan-chhupai and peek-a-boo in the flowering garden. Children listen and look at the textbook illustrations.

Whole-class discussion: Who is in Bela's family? Children share observations from the text. The teacher then opens the question outward — who is in your family? Children call out names and relationships freely; the teacher notes a variety of family sizes and structures on the board without ranking them.

Children open Textbook p. 6 and, guided by the discussion prompt there, talk in pairs about their own family members. Each child then draws a quick sketch of one family moment — playing, sitting together, or relaxing — in their notebook.

Three or four children share their sketches with the class. The teacher closes by naming what the class discovered: families look different from one another and all gather in different ways to enjoy time together.

periods.implied_lo: Students can describe family relationships and the ways family members spend time together.
periods.section_context: Bela's family — Banku Bhaiya, Bishu, the flowering garden, chhupan-chhupai, peek-a-boo, evening gatherings of relatives and neighbours.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'Does every family look the same as Bela's?' Welcome responses about single-parent homes, joint families, and families with grandparents — affirm all as equally whole. Keep the mood joyful and unhurried.

periods.textbook_anchor: Singing Together — Think of a rain song and sing it with friends in the class (p. 6)

time_bands.activity: The teacher briefly describes the rainy-day scene from the chapter — the garden shelter, antakshari, snakes and ladders, hot pakodas, tea, and Dadiji's songs. Children open Textbook p. 6 and read the folk rain song printed there together as a class.

The teacher invites children to think of any rain song, rhyme, or chant they know — from home, a grandparent, or their neighbourhood. In small groups, children share what they remember. One group volunteer leads their group's song or chant for the class.

Each child writes two or three lines of a rain song in their notebook — either one they know or one they make up. Children who prefer may draw a rainy-day scene instead and label it. The room is active with quiet humming and writing.
Children share their songs or drawings in a quick round. The teacher names what this activity shows: songs about rain travel from grandparents to children and keep memories of seasons alive.

periods.implied_lo: Students can express observations about seasonal experiences through oral and written creative modes.
periods.section_context: Rainy-day shelter, antakshari, snakes and ladders, pakodas, Dadiji's rain songs, folk rain song in textbook, oral transmission across generations.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'Where did Dadiji learn her rain songs? Who taught her?' This draws out naturally how songs and stories travel across generations without using the phrase 'oral tradition'. Invite songs in any language — regional songs are equally welcome.

periods.textbook_anchor: Singing Together — Write the names of family members in the table (p. 6)

time_bands.activity: The teacher revisits the discussion of Bela's family members from the opening section of the chapter, naming each person and their relationship. Children recall: Dadiji, Dadaji, parents, Banku Bhaiya, Bishu, and little Bishu.

Children open Textbook p. 6 and use the table format shown there to write the names of their own family members and each person's relationship to them. The teacher circulates, prompting children who are unsure about a relationship word.

Children share one entry from their table with a partner — name, relationship, and one thing that person does with or for them. Partners listen and ask one question. Then children add a detail or two to their own table entry based on the conversation.

The teacher invites a few children to read a name and relationship aloud. The class notices that families have different numbers of members and that the same relationship word (like 'grandmother') can point to very different people.

periods.implied_lo: Students can record and organise information about people in their immediate environment using a structured format.
periods.section_context: Bela's family members — Dadiji, Dadaji, parents, Banku Bhaiya, Bishu; table of family names and relationships.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Keep the tone warm and inclusive — some children may have step-parents, foster carers, or live with extended family only. Accept any person the child considers family. A quick look around the class at how many different family structures appear is a natural closing cue.

periods.textbook_anchor: Laughing Together — Find out what games grandparents used to play when they were young (p. 7)

time_bands.activity: The teacher reads the 'Laughing Together' section aloud, highlighting Dadaji playing traditional games alongside the children and the family's care for Shiru the dog. Children open Textbook p. 7 and look at the images.

Whole-class discussion: what games do children play with elders at home? The teacher then shares the task from Textbook p. 7 — finding out what games grandparents played when they were young. Children share any games they already know from elders: pittho, gilli-danda, kancha, hopscotch, kho-kho.

Children look at Textbook p. 8 and discuss: which animals come to your home or neighbourhood? Then: have you ever shared food with those animals? Children share experiences in pairs and report back. The class lists animals named — dogs, cows, cats, goats, parrots, buffaloes — on the board.

Brief reflection: why should we not hurt or tease animals? Children share reasons. The teacher draws out that animals who come to our homes are part of our wider family circle — cared for, not harmed.

periods.implied_lo: Students can connect personal experiences of play and animal care to broader ideas about intergenerational bonds and care for living beings.
periods.section_context: Dadaji playing traditional games, Shiru the dog, grandparents' games (pitthoo, gilli-danda, kancha), animals in the home and neighbourhood — dogs, cows, cats, goats, parrots, buffaloes, not hurting animals.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'Does your dada, dadi, nana, or nani play games with you? What do they call those games?' Regional names for the same game are common — welcome them all. If children have no living grandparents, invite them to ask an older neighbour or relative.

periods.textbook_anchor: Helping Each Other — Find out who does what work in your family and fill in the table (p. 15)

time_bands.activity: The teacher describes the 'Helping Each Other' section: Dadiji braids Bela's hair, parents share cooking and cleaning, Banku chops vegetables, Bela helps in the garden, and neighbour Kusum Mausi cooks festival sweets. Children open Textbook p. 9 and look at the activity showing household tasks.
Children use Textbook p. 9 to tick and colour the activities they see in their own family. The teacher circulates, asking children to name who does each task they have ticked.

Children turn to Textbook p. 15 and, using the table format, write down who does what work in their family — cooking, cleaning, gardening, shopping, care for elders or younger children, and any other task they notice. They aim for at least four different people and four different tasks.

Small group share: each child reads two entries. The class notices that work is spread across many members — children included — and that helping is a way of showing love. The teacher highlights that children's contributions matter.

periods.implied_lo: Students can observe and record the distribution of household work across family members, recognising children's contributions.
periods.section_context: Dadiji braiding hair, parents sharing cooking and cleaning, Banku chopping vegetables, Bela gardening, Kusum Mausi's festival sweets, household tasks table on p. 9, work distribution table on p. 15.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'Is there any work in your home that only one person does? Why do you think that is?' This opens a gentle, non-prescriptive conversation about division of labour without directing children to a fixed answer. Accept all observations.

periods.activity_title: Rangoli from Fallen Leaves and Flowers
periods.textbook_anchor: Helping Each Other — Collect fallen leaves and flowers and create a rangoli (p. 12)
materials: Fallen leaves and flowers collected from the school grounds
periods.visual_aids: Textbook illustration of Munni's rangoli made from dried flowers and leaves

time_bands.activity: The teacher reads about Munni making rangoli using colours from dried flowers and leaves, and about the tradition of making rangoli for festivals. Children open Textbook p. 12 and look at the illustration. The teacher explains that the class will collect fallen materials from the school grounds and make their own rangoli.

Children go to the school grounds in small groups (or the teacher pre-collects material if outdoor access is limited) and gather fallen leaves, petals, and flowers. They return to the classroom and spread their materials on newspaper sheets on the floor.

Each small group arranges their leaves and petals into a rangoli pattern on their newspaper sheet, without glue — a temporary arrangement as in the tradition. Children discuss the shapes and colours they are creating. Groups may look at each other's work for ideas.

A quick gallery walk: children move among the rangoli patterns. The teacher names what they have done — used natural, locally available materials to make something beautiful, as communities have done for generations.

periods.implied_lo: Students can use locally sourced natural materials to create a simple craft object, demonstrating a community making tradition.
periods.section_context: Munni's rangoli, dried flowers and leaves as colouring material, rangoli-making as a community craft tradition, fallen leaves and petals from school grounds.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'Have you seen rangoli being made at home or in your neighbourhood? What was it made from?' This brings out regional variations — rice flour, chalk, marigold petals, bricks — without privileging any single tradition. All are valid.

periods.activity_title: Drawing My Family and Their Relationships
periods.textbook_anchor: Helping Each Other — Draw a picture of family members and write relationships with them (p. 14)
periods.visual_aids: Textbook example of Bela's family relationship diagram on p. 13

time_bands.activity: Children open Textbook p. 13 and look at the activity showing Bela's relationships with all her family members. The teacher reads through the example, naming each relationship word. Children are then asked to look at Textbook p. 14 and prepare to draw their own family diagram.

Each child draws the members of their family and writes each person's relationship to themselves beneath each figure. Children who have fewer people at home may include neighbours or close friends who feel like family. The teacher circulates, helping with relationship words in the child's home language if needed.

Children share their drawing with a partner, pointing to each person and saying the relationship aloud. Partners ask one question about someone in the drawing — 'What does this person do with you?' — and the child answers.
The teacher closes by noting that every family diagram in the class looks different — different numbers, different relationships — and all of them show people who care for each other.

periods.implied_lo: Students can represent family structures and relationships visually, labelling each person's role.
periods.section_context: Bela's family relationship diagram, family members and relationship words, child's own family drawing and labelling, p. 13 example, p. 14 drawing task.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'Is there someone who feels like family to you even if they don't live in your house? Can they be in your drawing?' This opens the activity to children with non-traditional living arrangements. Keep the pace gentle and drawing-focused — an unhurried creative activity.

periods.activity_title: Pitthoo, Happy Moments, and Caring Beyond the Family
periods.textbook_anchor: Let us reflect — Draw some of the happy moments you enjoy together with your family (p. 17)
periods.visual_aids: Textbook illustration of the park outing and pitthoo game

time_bands.activity: The teacher describes Bela's family visit to the park: Dadaji joins the children in pitthoo — a team game using stacked stones and a ball — and the outing ends with ice cream and laughter. Children open the textbook and look at the illustration. The teacher explains pitthoo briefly: two teams, one knocks down a stack of stones, the other rebuilds it.

Discussion: what games do you play with your friends? Children share. The teacher then opens the 'Let us reflect' section (Textbook p. 17–18) and reads the discussion prompts aloud — what do you learn from elders? Who outside your family do you care for and how?

Children turn to Textbook p. 17 and draw one or two happy moments they enjoy with their family — an outing, a game, a meal, a celebration. Beneath or beside the drawing they write one sentence about it.

Children share their drawing and sentence with the class. The teacher closes the chapter by drawing out the big idea: families — and the friends, neighbours, and animals who are part of our lives — teach us to play, care, and belong together.

periods.implied_lo: Students can reflect on and express the values of care, participation, and belonging that connect family, friends, and community.
periods.section_context: Park outing, pitthoo game, stacked stones and ball, Dadaji playing with children, ice cream, 'Let us reflect' prompts — happy family moments drawing, intergenerational learning, care beyond the family.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'Who outside your family have you helped or been helped by this week?' This connects the chapter's theme of care to the child's actual daily life. Accept all answers — a shopkeeper, a neighbour, a school friend — as equally valid expressions of community care.

assessment_items.question_text: Bela and her brothers play chhupan-chhupai and peek-a-boo in their flowering garden. In the evenings, relatives, friends, and neighbours also come there. What does this tell us about Bela's family?

options.label: A
options.text: Bela's family only spends time with immediate family members.

options.label: B
options.text: Bela's family gathers with relatives, friends, and neighbours, making their home a place of togetherness.

options.label: C
options.text: Bela's family meets other people only during festivals.

options.label: D
options.text: Bela's brothers do not like playing outdoors.

assessment_items.annotation: The correct answer is B. This item checks whether the child grasped the chapter's opening idea that home and outdoor space become sites of wider community togetherness — not just immediate-family interaction.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can describe family relationships and the ways family members spend time together.

competency.competency_text: Describes relationships (including between humans and animals/nature) and traditions (art forms, celebrations, festivals) in the family and community

what_each_option_reveals.A: The child has limited the idea of 'family togetherness' to only immediate members, missing the text's description of relatives, friends, and neighbours gathering in the garden.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The child has confused the general evening-gathering pattern with festival-only occasions — a conflation of different sections of the chapter.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The child may have misread or not engaged with the opening description of Banku Bhaiya and Bishu playing outdoors with Bela.

assessment_items.task: Dadiji sings traditional songs about rain and has taught them to the children. Think of a rain song, rhyme, or chant you know — from home, a grandparent, or your neighbourhood. Write two or three lines of it in your notebook. If you do not know one, make up your own lines about rain.
assessment_items.scaffold:
My rain song / rhyme: ___________
Who taught it to me (or where I heard it): ___________
One thing this song makes me think of: ___________
format_of_output: Written lines of a rain song or rhyme
Note of who taught it or where it was heard
One sentence about what it brings to mind
assessment_items.annotation: Accept songs, rhymes, or chants in any language. Children who compose their own lines should be credited equally — the task values both memory and creativity. Regionally varied answers are acceptable and correct: rain songs differ widely across India and all are valid.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can express observations about seasonal experiences through oral and written creative modes.

competency.competency_text: Presents observations and findings through different creative modes (drawing, diagram, poem, play, skit, oral and written expression)

OPEN_TASK.what_this_demonstrates: The child can recall or create a song linked to a seasonal experience and present it in written form, connecting lived knowledge to a creative mode.
OPEN_TASK.reading_the_scaffold: The scaffold keeps the task in three moves: the song itself, its source, and one personal connection. A child who fills all three has shown full engagement; a child who fills one or two still demonstrates the core skill.
OPEN_TASK.strong_vs_weak_markers: Strong: a recognisable or original song with some seasonal imagery, a named source (grandparent, neighbour, mother), and a personal reflection. Weak: a single word or a drawing without any written expression of the song.
OPEN_TASK.inclusivity: Children who cannot write yet may dictate to the teacher or draw the rain scene and label it; oral sharing of the song is equally valid as the written product.
OPEN_TASK.format_rationale: The unit centred on expressing seasonal observations through song and writing — this task asks the child to perform that same creative act independently.

assessment_items.question_text: Look at the table you filled with your family members' names and relationships. Choose two people from your table and write: (a) their name, (b) their relationship to you, and (c) one thing they do with you or for you at home.
expected_elements: At least two family members named
The correct relationship word given for each (e.g., mother, grandfather, brother)
At least one specific activity or action that person does with or for the child
assessment_items.annotation: Relationship words may be given in English or in the child's home language — accept both. Regionally varied relationship terms (Nana/Dada, Chachi/Maami, etc.) are acceptable and correct. The activity the child mentions does not need to match the textbook — any genuine home activity is valid.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can record and organise information about people in their immediate environment using a structured format.

competency.competency_text: Explains the functioning of local institutions (family, school, bank/post office, market, and panchayat) in different forms (story, drawing, tabulating data, reports), and analyses their roles

expected_elements: At least two family members named
The correct relationship word given for each person
At least one specific activity or action that person does with or for the child at home

assessment_items.question_text: Dadaji plays traditional games with the children and everyone has fun together. Shiru the dog is also part of the family — fed and loved, not hurt. Which of the following best describes what this shows about Bela's family?

options.label: A
options.text: Only children and grandparents should play games together.

options.label: B
options.text: Animals should not be allowed inside a home.

options.label: C
options.text: Both elders and animals can be full members of a caring family circle.

options.label: D
options.text: Playing games is more important than caring for animals.

assessment_items.annotation: The correct answer is C. This item targets the dual idea in 'Laughing Together' — intergenerational play and the extension of family care to animals. Both themes appear in the same section and are deliberately paired in this item.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can connect personal experiences of play and animal care to broader ideas about intergenerational bonds and care for living beings.

competency.competency_text: Describes relationships (including between humans and animals/nature) and traditions (art forms, celebrations, festivals) in the family and community

what_each_option_reveals.A: The child has isolated only the grandparent–grandchild play detail and missed the chapter's broader point that all family members — of any age — participate together.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The child has drawn a conclusion opposite to the section's message; the text presents Shiru as a loved member of the household, not an outsider.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The child may have read the two themes (games, animals) as competing rather than as two expressions of the same caring relationship.

assessment_items.question_text: In Bela's home, everyone does some household work — Dadiji, parents, Banku, and Bela herself. Name three people in your family and write one task each of them does at home.
expected_elements: A distinct household task given for each person
At least one of the three tasks assigned to a child (the student or a sibling), showing children contribute
assessment_items.annotation: Accept any genuine household task — cooking, cleaning, gardening, shopping, caring for a younger sibling, fetching water, washing vessels. Regionally varied tasks (grinding spices, filling water from a well, milking animals) are acceptable and correct. The third expected element is a guide for the teacher, not a strict deduction criterion — if no child appears, probe gently.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can observe and record the distribution of household work across family members, recognising children's contributions.

competency.competency_text: Performs simple inquiry related to specific questions independently or in groups

expected_elements: A distinct household task given for each person
At least one of the three tasks attributed to a child or young person in the family

assessment_items.task: Munni made a beautiful rangoli using colours from dried flowers and leaves. Using fallen leaves, petals, or any natural material you find around you right now, arrange a small rangoli pattern on a sheet of paper. You do not need to glue anything — just place and arrange. When you finish, draw a quick sketch of your pattern in your notebook.
assessment_items.scaffold:
My rangoli sketch: [draw here]
Materials I used: ___________
Where I have seen rangoli being made: ___________
format_of_output: A physical arrangement of natural materials on paper (observed by teacher)
A drawn sketch of the pattern in the notebook
Written list of materials used and one note about where the child has seen rangoli made
assessment_items.annotation: The natural materials used will vary by season and school location — dry leaves, grass blades, flower petals, small stones, and seeds are all valid. Regionally varied answers are acceptable and correct: rangoli traditions differ across India in material, occasion, and name (kolam, alpana, aipan). Accept all. If the school grounds are inaccessible, provide a small collection of safe natural materials.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can use locally sourced natural materials to create a simple craft object, demonstrating a community making tradition.

competency.competency_text: Uses local materials to create simple objects (family tree, envelopes, origami animals) on their own for display or use in classroom processes

OPEN_TASK.what_this_demonstrates: The child can select locally available natural materials and arrange them intentionally into a pattern, connecting the act to a community craft tradition.
OPEN_TASK.reading_the_scaffold: The three scaffold prompts track: the visual product (sketch), the materials (connects to 'local'), and the cultural anchor (where they have seen it). A child who completes all three shows full engagement with both the making and the cultural dimension.
OPEN_TASK.strong_vs_weak_markers: Strong: a deliberate arrangement of at least two different materials, a recognisable pattern sketched, and a specific location named (grandparent's doorstep, a festival, a neighbour's home). Weak: a random scatter of one material type and a blank sketch.
OPEN_TASK.inclusivity: Children with limited fine motor control may describe their intended pattern verbally; a child who cannot access natural materials may draw an imagined rangoli using coloured pencils instead.
OPEN_TASK.format_rationale: The unit centred on using locally sourced materials to create a craft object — this task asks the child to perform that same making act and record it visually.

assessment_items.task: Draw the members of your family and write each person's relationship to you below their picture. Try to include at least three people. You can look at the example in your textbook on page 13 to help you.
assessment_items.scaffold:
My family drawing: [draw here]
Person 1 name: ___________ Relationship: ___________
Person 2 name: ___________ Relationship: ___________
Person 3 name: ___________ Relationship: ___________
(Add more if you like!)
format_of_output: Drawing of at least three family members
Relationship label written beneath each figure
Names written (may be in child's home language)
assessment_items.annotation: Accept any person the child considers family — close friends, neighbours, or carers are valid inclusions. Relationship words may be given in any language (Nani, Chachi, Bade Bhaiya). The drawing need not be detailed — stick figures with labels meet the criterion fully. Regionally varied relationship terms are acceptable and correct.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can represent family structures and relationships visually, labelling each person's role.

competency.competency_text: Presents observations and findings through different creative modes (drawing, diagram, poem, play, skit, oral and written expression)

OPEN_TASK.what_this_demonstrates: The child can organise knowledge about family members into a visual representation and attach the correct relationship label to each, showing both social understanding and the ability to communicate through drawing.
OPEN_TASK.reading_the_scaffold: The scaffold prompts the child through three named entries; the invitation to add more rewards children from larger families. A child who labels at least three people with correct relationship words has met the core expectation.
OPEN_TASK.strong_vs_weak_markers: Strong: at least three figures drawn and clearly labelled, relationship words correct or close, names present. Weak: a single figure with no label, or a drawing with no written component at all.
OPEN_TASK.inclusivity: Children who find drawing difficult may use a list format (Name — Relationship — one sentence about them) as an equivalent. Children who cannot yet write relationship words may dictate to the teacher.
OPEN_TASK.format_rationale: The unit asked children to draw their family members and write relationships — this task repeats that same creative recording act for independent assessment.

assessment_items.question_text: Dadaji played pitthoo with the children in the park, and the whole family — young and old — laughed and shared ice cream together. Think about your own life: who outside your family (a friend, neighbour, or anyone else) do you care for or who cares for you? Describe at least two ways in which you show care for each other.
look_for: Names or describes at least one person outside the immediate family who is part of their caring circle
Gives at least two specific, concrete examples of caring actions (helping, sharing food, checking on someone, playing together, offering comfort)
Shows understanding that care and belonging extend beyond blood relationships to community
Writes in their own voice with some personal detail, not a generic list
assessment_items.annotation: Accept any genuine caring relationship — a neighbour, a school friend, a shopkeeper, an animal the child cares for, or a community elder. Regionally varied answers are acceptable and correct: caring practices differ across communities and all are valid. Do not penalise for grammar or spelling in Grade III.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can reflect on and express the values of care, participation, and belonging that connect family, friends, and community.

competency.competency_text: Observes and describes cultural diversity in their immediate environment (food, clothing, games, different seasons, festivals related to harvest and sowing)

look_for: Names or describes at least one person outside the immediate family who is part of the child's caring circle
Provides at least two specific, concrete examples of caring actions that are mutual or reciprocal
Demonstrates that the child understands belonging and care as extending beyond blood relationships to friends, neighbours, and community
Writes with some personal detail and authenticity, not merely a textbook-echo
